analysis.one_liner: Expands what can be patented, making isolated human genes and many software processes patentable again.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one subcommittee hearing in January 2024, it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, sponsored by Senator Tillis and cosponsored by Senator Coons, would rewrite the rules for what kinds of inventions qualify for a patent. Today, courts can reject patents on things like abstract ideas, laws of nature, and genes as they exist in the body. The bill would wipe out those court-made limits and replace them with a short list of narrow exceptions, so far more inventions — including human genes that have been isolated from the body and many computer-implemented processes — would qualify for roughly 20-year exclusive rights. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, received a single subcommittee hearing, and never got a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that own or want patents — especially brand-name drug makers, biotech firms, gene-testing companies, and holders of software patents — would gain because more of their inventions would qualify for exclusive rights, and courts would lose their main tool for striking down overbroad patents on natural materials, diagnostics, and computer processes. Patent lawyers and litigants would also see more patentable subject matter and more disputes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patent-holding drug, biotech, and software companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill abolishes the judge-made exceptions courts have created to patent eligibility and replaces them with a short statutory list of exclusions, so inventions courts currently reject would become eligible for patents.

Under the bill, a human gene or natural material is not 'unmodified' if it has been 'isolated, purified, enriched, or otherwise altered by human activity' — meaning genes and natural products taken out of the body or purified would be patentable, reversing the practical effect of Supreme Court rulings that invalidated such patents.

The only exclusions would be narrow: standalone mathematical formulas, purely mental processes, processes occurring wholly in nature, unmodified genes and natural materials, and purely human business, social, or cultural steps — with anything that needs a machine or computer to perform still eligible.

analysis.who_pays: Patients and consumers would bear the cost through higher prices where new patents block generic drugs, genetic tests, and natural-product-based treatments. Software developers and businesses facing infringement suits would lose the early, low-cost way to defeat weak patents on abstract ideas, and companies wanting to use natural materials or gene sequences for research and testing could face new exclusive claims.

drawbacks.text: Because genes and natural materials count as 'modified' once isolated or purified, the bill would allow companies to claim exclusive patent rights over genetic sequences and natural compounds taken from nature, which can raise the price of medical tests and treatments built on them.

By eliminating all judge-made exceptions, the bill removes the main early defense courts use to dismiss overly broad software and diagnostic patents, increasing litigation costs for developers and businesses even though it keeps a carve-out for purely human business-method steps.

Stronger and broader patent eligibility tends to benefit whoever already holds large patent portfolios — often large pharmaceutical and technology companies — as much as or more than small independent inventors, since patents function as bargaining chips in negotiations and lawsuits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — clearer, more predictable rules for inventors frustrated by inconsistent court rulings — is legitimate, and some inventors would genuinely benefit from knowing their discoveries can be patented. But the design does this by removing the main check that keeps patents off things isolated from nature and off overly abstract processes, and the clearest beneficiaries are patent-rich drug, biotech, and technology companies rather than the public, which would face higher prices and more patent litigation. The bill offers little for ordinary people directly and carries real costs for them.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in January 2024, and died there without ever reaching a committee vote or the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 22, 2023 by Senator Tillis (for himself and Senator Coons) and read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Intellectual Property held a hearing on the bill on January 23, 2024, with a printed hearing record.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a committee markup or vote and never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current legal limits on patenting stay in place, which benefits patients, generic drug makers, medical laboratories, and software developers who would otherwise have faced new patent monopolies on isolated genes, natural materials, diagnostics, and computer-implemented processes. Patent-holding companies lose the broader rights the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients, generic makers, and software developers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead with one Democratic cosponsor (1 of 48 Senate Democrats) — but because the bill never reached a vote, there is no record of how the full Senate or either party would have divided.

industries.note: The bill would make purified natural products and isolated human genes patentable again, extending the exclusive rights these companies use to keep generic competition and competing tests off the market. The cost lands on patients through higher drug and testing prices.

Companies that patent isolated genes and diagnostic processes would gain exclusive control over tests; laboratories, researchers, and patients wanting to use those genes and methods would face licensing costs or blocked access.

industries.industry: Software patent holders and patent-assertion firms
industries.note: Wiping out the judge-made exceptions removes the fastest way defendants defeat broad software patents; the bill excludes only purely human business-method steps, so computer-implemented processes remain eligible. Developers and businesses facing suits would pay more to defend against weak patents.

More patentable subject matter and harder-to-dismiss claims mean more filings, prosecutions, and infringement disputes — more work for patent lawyers and litigation funders, paid for by parties sued and ultimately by consumers.
